opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one I think about a lot, both in my own work and when I'm coding. My rough rule of thumb is: if the task is well-defined, repetitive, and has a clear correct answer, I lean toward writing a deterministic tool. If it's fuzzy, open-ended, or involves natural language where the inputs vary a lot, that's where an LLM really shines.

To give a concrete example, say I need to convert a bunch of files from one format to another, or extract a specific field from structured data. I could ask an LLM to do it, and it would probably get it right most of the time. But "most of the time" is the key issue. A small Python script will do it correctly every time, it's cheaper, it's faster, and I can test it. There's no reason to introduce randomness into something that doesn't need it.

On the other hand, if I want to summarize a paper, classify free-form user feedback, or rephrase something, writing rules for that would be a nightmare. You'd end up with a giant pile of if-else statements that still breaks on edge cases. That's exactly the kind of problem these models were built for.

What I find interesting is that there's a nice middle ground now: you can use the LLM to help you *write* the deterministic tool. Instead of having the model do the task a thousand times, you have it write the script once, you review and test it, and then you just run the script. That gives you the best of both worlds. You get the flexibility and speed of the LLM during development, but the reliability and reproducibility of regular code at runtime.

There are also a few practical factors I weigh. One is cost and latency. If something runs millions of times, calling a large model every time adds up quickly. Another is verifiability. If I can't easily check whether the output is correct, I'm more cautious about handing it to an LLM, or I at least want some kind of check in the loop. And then there's the question of how often the task changes. If the requirements keep shifting, an LLM with a good prompt can be more adaptable than code you have to keep rewriting.

So in short: deterministic where you can, LLM where you must, and very often the LLM as a tool to build the deterministic thing. And of course, a lot of the agent-style systems we're seeing now are basically formalizing that idea, where the model decides when to call a calculator or run code instead of trying to do everything itself in its head.

r001.rationale: It contrasts having an LLM write a deterministic script once with having the LLM perform the task repeatedly.

r002.rationale: It recommends deterministic tools for well-defined tasks with clear correct answers, citing reliability, cost, and speed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot, actually, because I have this tendency, like many people right now, to reach for the LLM first just because it's convenient. And I've had to kind of consciously push back on that in my own work.

The way I think about it is, if the task has a well-defined, correct answer, and I can write down the rules for getting that answer, then I should probably just write the rules. Things like parsing a file format, computing some statistic, renaming variables across a codebase, validating inputs. Those are deterministic problems. If I use an LLM for that, I'm paying for something that's slower, more expensive, and occasionally wrong, when I could have something that's fast, free, and right every time. And the "occasionally wrong" part is the one that really matters, because it's the kind of wrong that's hard to catch. It'll look plausible.

Where the LLM makes sense is when the task is fuzzy. When the input is unstructured natural language, or when specifying the rules would take longer than the task itself, or when I genuinely can't enumerate all the cases. Summarizing a paper, classifying text where the categories are a bit subjective, drafting code where I'll review it anyway. Those are cases where "pretty good most of the time" is actually the right standard, because there often isn't a crisp notion of exactly right.

And then there's a middle ground I find really useful, which is using the LLM to help me build the deterministic tool. So instead of calling the model every time I need to parse something, I'll have it write the parser, I'll test the parser, and then I have a tool. That's often the best of both worlds. You get the flexibility of the model during development and the reliability of regular code in production.

One heuristic I use: if I'd be embarrassed when it fails, it should probably be deterministic. If a failure is just a slightly worse summary, fine, use the model. If a failure is a wrong number in a report or a silently corrupted dataset, I want code I can read and test. And honestly, I also think about how often it runs. Something I run once, I don't care, let the LLM do it. Something that runs a million times a day, the cost and latency add up and the error rate compounds, so that pushes me toward a tool.

So it's less of a binary decision for me and more like, how well-specified is the problem, what's the cost of being wrong, and how often does it run. And the answer tends to fall out of those three things.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes having the LLM write a parser that is tested and used as a tool from calling the model each time to perform the task.

r002.rationale: It recommends writing deterministic rules for well-defined tasks and says deterministic problems should use code rather than an LLM.

astra-6.text:
I usually start by asking, can I define the task precisely? If I can write down the rules and implement them reliably, I would generally use a deterministic tool. There’s no reason to have an LLM do a calculation that a few lines of Python can do exactly. The code is easier to test, and I know it will behave consistently.

Where an LLM becomes useful is when the input is ambiguous or unstructured—when understanding what somebody means is part of the task. For example, if you want to extract information from documents that all look different, writing rules for every variation can become very difficult.

And often you want both. The LLM can interpret the request and decide which tool to call, and then the tool does the actual computation. You can also use the LLM to help write that tool. If it’s a recurring task, generating code that you can inspect and test may be more useful than asking the model to solve the same problem from scratch every time.

So I’d look at how well specified the task is, how much variability there is, and what happens when the system makes a mistake. Those considerations usually tell you where the LLM adds value.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes having the LLM help write a tool from asking the model to solve the task each time, and describes the LLM interpreting requests while a tool performs the computation.

r002.rationale: It recommends a deterministic tool when the task can be precisely defined and reliably implemented, citing exact calculations as an example.

sol-6.1.text:
I usually start by asking: can I clearly specify the rules for this task? If I can, and I need the same input to always produce the same output, I would probably write a regular program. There’s no reason to introduce the cost and uncertainty of an LLM into something a few lines of code can do reliably.

An LLM becomes useful when the input is ambiguous or unstructured—when you’re working with natural language and it’s difficult to enumerate all the possible ways someone might express something. But then I also ask: how do I check whether the output is correct? How expensive is a mistake?

And often it’s a combination. You can have the LLM interpret a request and select a tool, but let deterministic code do the calculation or execute the operation. Or use the LLM to help you develop that code in the first place. Using an LLM to solve a problem doesn’t necessarily mean you need to keep an LLM in the final system.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes an LLM interpreting or performing a task from using an LLM to help develop code that performs it, and says the LLM need not remain in the final system.

r002.rationale: It recommends a regular program when the rules are clear and the same input should always produce the same output.
